prompt: Of Coreto's engineering budget of R$ 17,384,000 a year, what share is the people line?

choices.why: That is the cloud line, the invoice engineers see most, and the second line rather than the first.
That is the other three lines added together: cloud, licences and tooling.
Right: R$ 13,728,000 of R$ 17,384,000. Four fifths of the budget is people's time.
A guess at an even split. The sheet puts people far above half.

prompt: Ask an engineer at Coreto what engineering costs and they name the cloud bill. Why that line, by the lesson?
hint: Which costs arrive as an invoice?

choices.text: It is the largest line of the budget
choices.why: It is the second line. People are 79.0% of the budget against the cloud's 14.6%.

choices.text: The CFO reports it to the board every month
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so, and it would not explain what engineers notice.

choices.text: Cloud spend is the line engineers decide alone, without finance
choices.why: Engineers decide much of how their own hours are spent too; that is the larger line.

choices.text: It is an invoice engineers see; salaries arrive as none
choices.why: Right: the biggest cost never arrives as an invoice, so the people closest to it rarely count it.

prompt: C2 holds =ROUND(B2/SUM($B$2:$B$5)*100,1) and is copied down to C5. What do the dollar signs do?
hint: What would C5 divide by without them?

choices.text: They format the result as currency
choices.why: A dollar sign inside a cell reference has nothing to do with money; formatting is set on the cell.

choices.text: They round the share to one decimal place
choices.why: ROUND does that, with its second argument. The dollar signs are in the range.

choices.text: They keep the range on rows 2 to 5 in every copy
choices.why: Right: without them the range slides a row per copy and C5 divides by a sum that includes empty cells.

choices.text: They make the cell read-only so nobody edits the total by mistake
choices.why: Protecting a cell is a separate feature. The dollar signs change how a reference is copied.

prompt: Coreto cancels a hosted log service and runs an open-source one on its own machines. The licence line falls. What does the lesson say about the total?

choices.text: Part of it reappears as operating hours on the people line
choices.why: Right: a licence replaces people's time, so cancelling one moves cost to a line where nobody books it to the decision.

choices.text: It falls by the licence saved
choices.why: That reads one line as if it were the budget. The operating hours land somewhere else.

choices.text: It rises, because open source costs more than a licence
choices.why: The lesson does not rank them in general; it says the cost moves, and the sum decides.

choices.text: The cloud line absorbs it, since the machines are in the cloud
choices.why: Some machine cost lands there, but the large part lesson 9 found was people's time.

prompt: Match each budget line to how fast the lesson says it can change.
hint: A role takes months to fill.

prompt: A 10% cut of Coreto's R$ 17,384,000 budget is how many engineers, at R$ 264,000 an engineer-year? One decimal place.
Otávio settles for a 5% cut instead, taken as a hiring freeze from July to December. How many roles must stay empty for those six months? One decimal place.
hint: 5% of the budget in engineer-years, then remember each frozen role saves half a year.

prompt: The first answer in the room is "trim the cloud, review the licences". Why does the sheet say that cannot cover the 10%?
hint: Compare R$ 1,738,400 with what is not people.

choices.text: Cloud providers forbid cutting a contract mid-year
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson rests on contracts; the size of the cut is the problem.

choices.text: Licences are fixed for three years
choices.why: The lesson says licences change at renewal, yearly in Coreto's case; it is still too small a line.

choices.text: Saving on the cloud slows the site down
choices.why: That is a fear, and not the lesson's argument; the argument is arithmetic.

choices.text: It is 68% of the cloud bill, 47.5% of all that is not people
choices.why: Right: R$ 1,738,400 against R$ 2,544,000 of cloud and R$ 3,656,000 outside the payroll. The numbers do not fit.

prompt: Which of these are ways the lesson says a cut lands on the people line? Choose all that apply.
hint: Who does the work next year.

choices.text: Open roles left unfilled
choices.why: Yes: the first of the three, and the quietest.

choices.text: Moving staging to smaller machines
choices.why: That is a cloud saving, the line lesson 12 reads.

choices.text: People who leave and are not replaced
choices.why: Yes: the team shrinks as people go, one desk at a time.

choices.text: Renegotiating the licence contracts at renewal
choices.why: That touches the licence line, which is 4.2% of the budget.

prompt: Davi's option A takes the cut from the microservices migration and the front-end framework. Why there, by the lesson?
hint: What did the strategy already say about that work?

choices.text: The strategy had already postponed them
choices.why: Right: the policy says where a cut may not land, and the list of what Coreto will not do says where it hurts least.

choices.text: They are the most expensive projects
choices.why: Cost is not the reason given; the strategy's choices are.

choices.text: Their teams are the newest, so the losses are smallest
choices.why: Nothing about team age appears in the lesson; the choice follows the strategy.

choices.text: Cutting a little from every team spreads the pain fairly
choices.why: The lesson calls that what a team with no strategy does: it spreads the damage across every priority.

prompt: Put the six questions of a request for money in the order the lesson answers them.
hint: Start with where it sits in the budget.
trap: Leading with the return, before the line and the amount, leaves the reader nowhere to put it in the budget.

prompt: Which question does the lesson say engineering requests leave out most often, and a CFO checks first?
hint: Most requests are for people already on the payroll.

choices.text: How much it costs
choices.why: Requests name a cost readily; what they skip is what gives way to it.

choices.text: Which technology it uses
choices.why: The usual request is full of technology; that is the habit the lesson corrects.

choices.text: Who approved it before
choices.why: Not one of the six questions, and not what a finance reader is missing.

choices.text: What waits because this happens
choices.why: Right: moving people is still a cost, paid in whatever they stop doing.

prompt: Davi's sentence for Otávio: R$ ___ of work to stop paying R$ 120,900 a year.
hint: The principal lesson 5 priced: 320 hours at R$ 150.

prompt: Davi's request mentions the failed on-sales in words and puts no amount on them. How does the lesson judge that?

choices.text: As a gap that weakens the request
choices.why: The lesson treats it as a strength: an unpriced risk said plainly beats an invented number.

choices.text: As honest: that part is not priced yet, and it says so
choices.why: Right: lesson 20 puts a probability and an amount on it. Until then, saying so keeps trust for the next request.

choices.text: As a mistake: Davi should estimate a figure to win the case
choices.why: An inflated figure spends trust; the CFO who finds one discounts every number after it.

choices.text: As irrelevant, since the interest alone justifies the team
choices.why: The lesson calls the interest the smaller part of the case; the on-sales are what make it urgent.

prompt: A small company's cloud bill is larger than its payroll. Which claim from this lesson would you have to check again before applying it there?
hint: Which claim rests on Coreto's shares?

choices.text: A request needs a line, an amount and a date
choices.why: That holds wherever there is a budget; it does not depend on the shares.

choices.text: Most of a real cut lands on people
choices.why: Right: that follows from people being 79.0% at Coreto. With the cloud as the largest line, the arithmetic changes.

choices.text: A cut decided mid-year saves only the months left
choices.why: That is about the calendar, and it holds whatever the shares are.

choices.text: Cancelling a licence moves cost to people's time
choices.why: That depends on what the licence replaced, not on the size of the payroll.

prompt: What share of the R$ 1,738,400 cut would cancelling every licence and subscription (R$ 732,000 a year) cover? Whole percent.
Two engineers spend a quarter on a cloud-saving project. What does the saving have to exceed before the project has paid for itself?

choices.text: R$ 264,000, one engineer-year
choices.why: Two engineers for a quarter is half an engineer-year, not a whole one.

choices.text: Zero, because their salaries are paid anyway
choices.why: Paid anyway, but spent on this instead of something else; that is the cost the lesson prices.

choices.text: R$ 132,000 of their time
choices.why: Right: 2 × R$ 264,000 ÷ 4. The hours are priced the same way as the invoice.

choices.text: R$ 66,000, one engineer for a quarter
choices.why: That counts one of the two engineers.

prompt: Helena meets the 10% by freezing 6.6 roles from July. At the end of the year, how much has she actually cut?
hint: Each frozen role saves half a year.

choices.text: The full 10%: 6.6 engineers
choices.why: That counts the roles as if frozen from January. Six months of each was spent before July.

choices.text: Nothing, because roles not yet filled cost nothing
choices.why: The budget planned for them, so leaving them empty does save money, for the months it lasts.

choices.text: 3.3 engineer-years: half the cut
choices.why: Right: the calendar halves it, which is how a 10% cut becomes 5% on the books.

choices.text: 13.2 engineer-years, twice the cut
choices.why: 13.2 is the number of roles a mid-year freeze needs to reach 6.6 engineer-years, not the saving.

prompt: Cancelling a licence moves its cost to the ___ line of the budget.
hint: Somebody now does the work the licence did.
